newsitem.title: USA: Teamster chief Carey has early lead against Hoffa.
newsitem.headline: Teamster chief Carey has early lead against Hoffa.

text.p: The self-styled reformer who heads the biggest U.S. union took an early lead on Wednesday in a quest to keep his job and defeat challenger James Hoffa, son of the union leader who made the Teamsters synonymous with labour corruption.
Teamster President Ron Carey took an early lead as head of the 1.4 million-member union, but votes from Hoffa's stronghold had yet to be counted.

With less than three percent of the mail-in ballots from 14 locals tallied at midday in the first full day of counting, local-by-local results provided by a court-appointed election officer showed Carey leading Hoffa by 8,192 to 6,169.
But the early results did not include votes from the Midwest, considered the powerbase of Hoffa, a Detroit labour lawyer and son of legendary Teamster leader Jimmy Hoffa.
Election observers for Carey's campaign, however, had tallied 25 locals by midday, with Carey leading by 17,457 to 9,877. Those results included two midwestern locals.
Despite the early lead, Carey campaign staffers said it was too soon to spot a voter trend in the data. The awesome task of counting some 500,000 ballots was expected to take the rest of the week.
"We're still saying this is a horse race," Carey campaign spokeswoman Renee Asher said. "There's a long way to go. There isn't a trend yet."
The Hoffa campaign had viewed the higher turnout in this election as a positive sign for the challenger.

Both campaigns had predicted a close race, a rare point of agreement among two bitter enemies, each of whom has accused the other of being corrupt, tied to unsavory characters, inept and unfit for a job that has a larger constituency than any two members of the House of Representatives.
Hoffa, 55, whose father is presumed to have been murdered by the mob in 1975, has worked for the past three years for a Teamster joint council that was once headed by his father.
Carey, 60, a former United Parcel Service driver and dissident leader of a New York local, is a self-styled reformer who won his office as the darkhorse candidate in a three-way race in 1991.

The current election is only the second in the 93-year history of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters that has been open to all rank-and-file members. Previous presidents of the union that for years was the symbol of labour corruption were elected by convention delegates.

But in 1989 the union that saw three of its last six presidents go to prison settled a federal anti-racketeering suit by agreeing to hold open elections run by the government. The settlement also installed a panel of overseers with broad investigatory authority for an indefinite period of time.

The government has budgeted about $21 million for this election, which includes the cost of its vote-counting facility here and a temporary staff of 500 workers. The union picked up the tab for the 1991 election.
In the last election, only about 425,000 votes were cast by the union's 1.4 million members, but more than 28,000 were not counted because of voter error or candidate challenges.
